final_proof:
Let \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). For each \(a\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), put
\[
S_a=\{i\in I:x_{a,i}\ne0\},\qquad S=\bigcup_{a=1}^m S_a.
\]
Each \(S_a\) is countable by the definition of \(A\), and a finite union of countable sets is countable. Hence there is an injection \(\phi:S\to\mathbb N_0\).

We first record why relabeling by \(\phi\) preserves the sums used below. Suppose \((c_i)_{i\in I}\) is a nonnegative family which vanishes off \(S\) and has finite generalized sum. Define \(z_n=c_i\) when \(n=\phi(i)\) for some \(i\in S\), and set \(z_n=0\) when \(n\notin\phi(S)\). Then
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z_n=\sum_{i\in I}c_i. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, both sides equal the supremum of \(\sum_{i\in F}c_i\) over finite subsets \(F\subseteq S\). For the generalized sum this follows from its definition as the limit of the increasing net of finite subsums. Every initial partial sum of the series is one such finite subsum. Conversely, every finite \(F\subseteq S\) satisfies \(\phi(F)\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N\}\) for some \(N\), so its sum is at most the corresponding initial partial sum. This proves (1).

For each \(a=1,\ldots,m\), define \(y_a=(y_{a,n})_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
y_{a,n}=\begin{cases}
x_{a,i},&n=\phi(i)\text{ for some }i\in S,\\
0,&n\notin\phi(S).
\end{cases}
\]
This is well-defined because \(\phi\) is injective. Applying (1) to \(c_i=x_{a,i}^2\) gives
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}y_{a,n}^2
 =\sum_{i\in I}x_{a,i}^2<\infty.
\]
Thus \(y_a\in\ell^2\).

Fix \(a,b\in\{1,
\ldots,m\}\). The family \(((x_{a,i}-x_{b,i})^2)_{i\in I}\) vanishes off \(S\). Moreover, for every finite \(F\subseteq I\),
\[
\sum_{i\in F}(x_{a,i}-x_{b,i})^2
\le 2\sum_{i\in F}x_{a,i}^2+2\sum_{i\in F}x_{b,i}^2
\le 2\sum_{i\in I}x_{a,i}^2+2\sum_{i\in I}x_{b,i}^2.
\]
Its net of finite subsums is therefore increasing and bounded, so it converges in \(\mathbb R\). Applying (1) to this squared-difference family yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\ell^2}(y_a,y_b)^2
 &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(y_{a,n}-y_{b,n})^2\\
 &=\sum_{i\in I}(x_{a,i}-x_{b,i})^2
 =d_2(x_a,x_b)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both distances are nonnegative, hence
\[
d_{\ell^2}(y_a,y_b)=d_2(x_a,x_b).
\]

Finally, the construction preserves equality exactly. If \(x_a=x_b\), then clearly \(y_a=y_b\). Conversely, if \(x_a\ne x_b\), choose \(i\in I\) such that \(x_{a,i}\ne x_{b,i}\). Then \(i\in S_a\cup S_b\subseteq S\), and
\[
y_{a,\phi(i)}=x_{a,i}\ne x_{b,i}=y_{b,\phi(i)},
\]
so \(y_a\ne y_b\). Thus, for every \(a,b\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), both required assertions hold.
